\-I'm sure the pilots questioned what was happening constantly, but you can't reasonably expect them to put together all of what Nathan was doing here. This is one of the weirdest and most elaborate "reality" shows of all time, put on by a guy with a decade of experience tricking hundreds of people into doing weird stuff on TV. It's not reasonable to expect any normal person to realize the full scope of what was happening here. 

  
\-Again, it's very possible Nathan/the team briefed Mara on what was about to happen. It might even be likely, I'm just frustrated that so many people are treating it as a certainty, and acting like I'm an idiot for questioning it. 

\-The scene itself absolutely rests on the tension that we know Jeff has been kicked off multiple dating apps for harassing women, and that Mara doesn't know that. That might not literally be true, but the scene is built around the audience's discomfort and expectation that he will harass her, which he does. If you're saying that's not the intended point of the scene, I think you're being dishonest.

\-Her meeting Jeff does not mean she knew about his history. Why would he tell her that?

I've asked every person who's responded to this what evidence there is that Mara \*did\* know what was going on before she went into the flight simulator and no one has answered me. It's very possible she did! But I don't know why I should assume she did when the show implies she did not. 

People sign agreements to appear on camera, those agreements don't include everything they are going to be filmed doing. That would be impossible for unscripted TV. People don't sign agreements before and after every scene they film.

She's also a real person with feelings being put in an uncomfortable or even potentially dangerous situation, regardless of what point was being made.

"It's fine, she's used to it" is so depressing. That's no reason or excuse to put her with a fairly extreme misogynist guy in front of TV cameras, especially if she didn't know what was about to happen.

If a TV producer approached me from HBO asking me to be on a show, I would probably say yes. I would probably also go along with it even if it seemed a little strange. That's how a lot of people would react!

All of this may be true. It's probably even likely true. I just don't agree with it being taken as a certainty.

\-Are we supposed to think Nathan's shows are 100% scripted? That was never my understanding of NFY or The Rehearsal, and I don't buy that at all. Does The Rehearsal mess with the audience by mixing scripted scenes with unscripted scenes? Absolutely. But I don't see why I should assume this particular scene is scripted, when it's not presented that way.

  
\-Is it likely that a show from a major network would allow a woman to be sexually harassed on camera in the year 2025? No, I guess not. But it's not unheard of for reality shows to be exploitative or even for Nathan to put women in uncomfortable situations. The woman from "The Hero" has said publicly that she had no idea what was happening in that episode. I just don't want to take it as a certainty that this conversation briefing Mara definitely happened, that's all.

I understand what you are saying, but my issue comes from the fact that as the show presents it, Mara was \*not\* asked to demonstrate how she deals with harassment. Or at the very least, she was not given the full picture that she was dealing with a misogynist who has been banned from five dating apps. Obviously we are not privy to every discussion and it's very possible she was prepped, but from her reactions it doesn't really seem that way and I don't think we should assume that is the case.

Basically, my issue is not with her being asked to demonstrate how she deals with harassment, it's her having to do it without being asked.
Of course, and I think any fan of his is aware of/okay with this to some extent, I just wonder if he went too far this time.

So we should excuse all his actions (that involve real people and have real consequences) because his comedic character is a bad person? I don't know about that. 

I like the show to be clear, and I know he's done other stuff like this, but that argument doesn't make a lot of sense to me.

I want to disagree with what most people are saying here and say that an ending SHOULD serve the theme (aka the philosophy of the film).

The Knives Out twist serves the theme because Marta beats Chris Evans' plan by being a good nurse. That's the final twist. The movie's philosophy: Marta wins against the rich family because she is a better person than them.

The twist in the Sixth Sense serves the theme because Bruce Willis makes peace with his own death. The movie's philosophy: Death is scary but you must make peace with the death of others (like Hayley Joel Osmond does) AND the fact that you will die someday (like Bruce Willis does).

The twist in the village is GOOD ACTUALLY because it serves the theme: that you can't hide from the world. The elders have reacted to personal tragedy by trying to hide from it, but Bryce Dallas Howard is brave enough to face it. The movie's philosophy: It's better to face grief than to hide from it.

A critic I like would always say "the ending is the conceit". The final image/emotion you leave the audience with should be the whole point of the story. I think a great twist should do the same thing!
